settle.simple: To go and live in a place and make it a lasting home.
settle.detailed: In HASS, people settle when they stay in a new area, build homes, and start a community. In Australian history this often happened on Country already cared for by First Nations peoples.
settle.zh: 定居；在某地安顿下来并长期居住
settle.example: Many families from Britain chose to settle near rivers because the soil was good for farming.
settle.basic: They went to live by the river.

spread.simple: To move outwards and cover a wider area.
spread.detailed: In science, heat, light, disease, or a substance can spread from one place to another. You watch how far and how fast it travels.
spread.example: Heat can spread along the metal spoon and warm your fingers at the other end.
spread.basic: The heat moved along the spoon.

struggle.simple: To try very hard when something is difficult.
struggle.detailed: In stories, a character may struggle against weather, fear, or another person. The effort matters as much as the result.
struggle.example: In the camp narrative, the lost walker had to struggle through wet scrub before reaching the track.
struggle.basic: The walker found the bush hard going.

succeed.simple: To achieve the result you set out to do.
succeed.detailed: You succeed when a plan, test, or goal works as intended. Scholarship writing often asks what helped a person or method succeed.
succeed.example: Oliver will succeed in the inquiry if he backs every claim with a clear source.
succeed.basic: He will do well if he uses sources.

survive.simple: To stay alive through danger, hardship, or change.
survive.detailed: Living things survive when they get what they need and cope with threats such as drought, fire, or predators.
survive.zh: 存活；幸存；熬过危险或艰苦
survive.example: Some eucalypts survive a bushfire because new shoots grow from protected buds.
survive.basic: Some trees stay alive after a fire.

suspect.simple: To think something is likely, even without full proof.
suspect.detailed: A reader may suspect a character is hiding the truth from clues in dialogue or action. You still need evidence before you treat the idea as fact.
suspect.zh: 怀疑；猜想某事可能属实
suspect.example: Readers start to suspect the narrator is leaving out the real reason she left camp.
suspect.basic: Readers think the narrator is hiding something.

symbolise.simple: To stand for an idea using an object, colour, or action.
symbolise.detailed: Writers symbolise feelings or themes so a simple image carries extra meaning, such as a wilting plant standing for lost hope.
symbolise.zh: 象征；用事物代表某种意义
symbolise.example: In Mia's poem, the empty water tank can symbolise a town waiting for rain.
symbolise.basic: The empty tank stands for waiting.

threaten.simple: To put someone or something in danger, or to warn of harm.
threaten.detailed: A drought can threaten crops, and a speaker can threaten a group with a penalty. In HASS, look at who has power and what is at risk.
threaten.example: Rising salt levels threaten farmland along parts of the Murray River.
threaten.basic: Salt is bad for the farms.

tolerate.simple: To accept something you dislike without fighting it.
tolerate.detailed: Communities tolerate different customs when people can live together fairly. It does not mean you must agree with every idea.
tolerate.zh: 容忍；宽容；接受自己并不喜欢的事物
tolerate.example: A fair classroom must tolerate honest disagreement so long as no one is belittled.
tolerate.basic: The class lets people disagree politely.

trade.simple: To exchange goods, services, or ideas with others.
trade.detailed: People trade when both sides give something and receive something. Australian colonies traded wool, gold, and food with other places.
trade.example: Coastal towns used to trade wool and wheat for tools brought by sailing ships.

transport.simple: To move people or goods from one place to another.
transport.detailed: Roads, railways, rivers, and ships transport freight and passengers. HASS inquiries ask how new transport changed towns and trade.
transport.zh: 运输；把人或货物从一地运到另一地
transport.example: The new railway could transport wheat to the port far faster than bullock wagons.
transport.basic: The train moved the wheat to the port.

trust.simple: To believe a person or idea is honest and reliable.
trust.detailed: Characters trust someone when they share secrets or follow advice. A broken promise can change the whole mood of a story.
trust.zh: 信任；信赖某人诚实可靠
trust.example: By the last chapter, readers no longer trust the charming guide who hid the map.

urge.simple: To strongly encourage someone to take a particular action.
urge.detailed: In persuasive writing you urge an audience toward a choice by giving reasons, not by shouting. A mayor might urge residents to save water.
urge.zh: 力劝；敦促某人采取行动
urge.example: In the waste debate, speakers urge the school to ban single-use plastic at the canteen.
urge.basic: Speakers want the school to drop plastic.

weigh.simple: To measure how heavy something is on a scale.
weigh.detailed: In an investigation you weigh a sample on a scale or balance so you can compare masses fairly and record accurate data.
weigh.example: Before the creek test, the group had to weigh each soil sample on the same balance.
weigh.basic: They checked how heavy the soil was.

absorb.simple: To take in liquid, heat, or energy the way a sponge takes in water.
absorb.detailed: A material can absorb water, sound, or sunlight. Dark cloth absorbs more heat than pale cloth, which is why playground seats feel hotter.
absorb.example: The black paper will absorb more sunlight than the white paper in the same tray.
absorb.basic: The black paper takes in more sun.

decay.simple: To break down slowly and lose strength or freshness.
decay.detailed: Food, wood, and teeth can decay when microbes or weather damage them over time. Scientists record how fast the change happens.
decay.example: Apple pieces decay faster in the warm compost than in the fridge.
decay.basic: The apple bits go bad more quickly outside.

decompose.simple: To break into simpler parts, often with help from living microbes.
decompose.detailed: Leaves and food scraps decompose when bacteria and fungi turn them into soil nutrients. It is a key step in many natural cycles.
decompose.zh: 分解；在微生物作用下变成更简单的物质
decompose.example: By term four, the garden scraps should decompose into dark, crumbly compost.
decompose.basic: The scraps will turn into compost.

imitate.simple: To copy the way someone speaks, acts, or writes.
imitate.detailed: Young writers sometimes imitate a favourite author's sentence patterns to learn craft. In a story, a character may imitate another person to tease or to fit in.
imitate.zh: 模仿；照着别人的样子做
imitate.example: For Book Week, the class tried to imitate Banjo Paterson's galloping rhythm without copying a whole poem.
imitate.basic: They tried to write in a similar rhythm.

counter.simple: To answer a claim with an opposite point.
counter.detailed: In a debate you counter an idea by giving a reason that weakens it. A fair speaker still treats the other side accurately.
counter.example: Aisha used recycling figures to counter the claim that students would not sort their rubbish.

refute.simple: To show that a claim is wrong using clear evidence.
refute.detailed: You refute an idea when your facts leave little room for it to stand. It is stronger than simply disagreeing.
refute.zh: 驳斥；用证据证明某说法不成立
refute.example: The water-test results refute the rumour that the creek is too dirty for yabbies.
refute.basic: The results show the rumour is wrong.

commence.simple: To begin something in a planned or formal way.
commence.detailed: Schools, inquiries, and ceremonies commence at a set time. The word sounds more official than everyday 'start'.
commence.example: The scholarship reading paper will commence after the supervisor checks every desk.
commence.basic: The test will start after desks are checked.

cease.simple: To stop happening or to stop doing something.
cease.detailed: Rain may cease after a storm, or a council may cease a noisy activity. The word marks a clear end, not a pause.
cease.example: Play must cease the moment the siren sounds so the oval can be cleared.
cease.basic: Play has to stop when the siren goes.

prioritise.simple: To treat the most important task or idea first.
prioritise.detailed: When time is short, you prioritise work that will have the biggest effect. Good notes show what you put first and why.
prioritise.zh: 优先处理；把最重要的事放在前面
prioritise.example: For the group project, we should prioritise the graph before decorating the poster.
prioritise.basic: We should do the graph first.

specialise.simple: To focus on one area and become especially skilled in it.
specialise.detailed: A scientist may specialise in insects, and a writer may specialise in mystery stories. Narrow focus can produce deeper knowledge.
specialise.zh: 专门从事；专攻某一领域
specialise.example: In Year 6, some students already specialise in coding while others explore several clubs.
specialise.basic: Some students stick to one main interest.

familiarise.simple: To make yourself know a place, text, or idea well.
familiarise.detailed: Before a test or excursion you familiarise yourself with the map, rules, or key words so fewer surprises slow you down.
familiarise.zh: 使熟悉；让自己了解某事物
familiarise.example: Please familiarise yourself with the library catalogue before Monday's research lesson.
familiarise.basic: Please get to know the catalogue first.

generalise.simple: To make a broad statement from a few examples.
generalise.detailed: Scientists generalise carefully after several trials. A weak writer may generalise from one story and treat it as a rule for everyone.
generalise.zh: 概括；从个别例子推出普遍说法
generalise.example: You cannot generalise about all birds from watching one magpie on the oval.
generalise.basic: One magpie does not prove a rule for every bird.

minimise.simple: To make something as small or as slight as possible.
minimise.detailed: In science and design you minimise waste, error, or risk by changing a method. The aim is a smaller unwanted effect, not zero thinking.
minimise.example: We changed the funnel design to minimise spills during the oil-and-water test.
minimise.basic: We changed the funnel so less liquid spilled.

maximise.simple: To make something as large or as strong as possible.
maximise.detailed: You maximise a result when you adjust conditions to get the greatest useful effect, such as more sunlight on a solar panel.
maximise.zh: 使增加到最大；尽量提高
maximise.example: The class tilted the panels to maximise sunlight during the winter midday test.
maximise.basic: They tilted the panels to catch more sun.

realise.simple: To become clearly aware of a fact or idea.
realise.detailed: You realise something when understanding clicks into place after clues, results, or reflection. It is more than guessing.
realise.example: Halfway through the proof, Maya began to realise the missing step was in the first line.
realise.basic: Maya finally saw the missing step.

civilise.simple: To try to make a society match one group's idea of 'proper' order.
civilise.detailed: Older texts used civilise as if some cultures were unfinished. Australian HASS now treats the word carefully because it judged First Nations societies unfairly.
civilise.zh: 使文明化（旧时带偏见，现需审慎理解）
civilise.example: Our HASS booklet asks why some colonists claimed they could civilise people who already had law and culture.
civilise.basic: Some colonists said their way of life was better.

authorise.simple: To give official permission for an action.
authorise.detailed: A council, principal, or parliament can authorise a plan so it is allowed by the rules. Without that permission the action may be unlawful.
authorise.example: Only the principal can authorise an excursion that leaves the school grounds.
authorise.basic: Only the principal can allow that trip.

standardise.simple: To make things follow the same agreed rule or measure.
standardise.detailed: Scientists standardise a method so every group uses the same steps and units. That makes results fairer to compare.
standardise.zh: 使标准化；统一做法或标准
standardise.example: We need to standardise the timing so every group stirs the mixture for two minutes.
standardise.basic: Everyone should stir for the same time.

characterise.simple: To describe the typical qualities of a person, place, or text.
characterise.detailed: You characterise a hero as brave or a setting as bleak by pointing to details. The word also means those qualities are typical of something.
characterise.example: Short, snapped sentences characterise the panic in the last scene of the camp story.
characterise.basic: The last scene feels panicked because the sentences are short.

advantage.simple: A feature that helps you or makes one option stronger than another.
advantage.detailed: In an argument, an advantage is a real gain, such as lower cost or greater safety. Name it clearly and show who benefits.
advantage.example: One advantage of the new bins is that food scraps no longer sit in the classroom.
advantage.basic: The new bins help because scraps are gone.

agreement.simple: A shared decision that people accept and follow.
agreement.detailed: An agreement can be a handshake, a class rule, or a written treaty. HASS texts ask who signed, who was left out, and whether it was kept.
agreement.example: The two classes reached an agreement about sharing the oval at lunch.
agreement.basic: The two classes decided how to share the oval.

aim.simple: The result you are trying to achieve on purpose.
aim.detailed: An aim is the target of a lesson, experiment, or piece of writing. Keep it short enough that you can check whether you met it.
aim.zh: 目标；意图；想要达成的结果
aim.example: The aim of our investigation was to find which material kept ice solid the longest.
aim.basic: We wanted to see which material kept ice frozen.

alternative.simple: Another possible choice instead of the first idea.
alternative.detailed: An alternative is a real option you can take. Strong arguments compare at least one alternative, not only the plan you already like.
alternative.example: A reusable bottle is a practical alternative to buying juice in the canteen each day.
alternative.basic: You could take a bottle instead of buying juice.

argument.simple: A reasoned case for a claim, backed by reasons and evidence.
argument.detailed: An argument is not a shouting match. In scholarship writing it has a clear position, supporting points, and a response to the other side.
argument.example: Her argument for a quieter library used noise counts from three lunchtimes.
argument.basic: She gave reasons for a quieter library.

audience.simple: The people who watch, listen to, or read a text.
audience.detailed: Writers change tone and detail to suit an audience. A speech for Year 1 sounds different from a letter to the local council.
audience.example: The play's audience gasped when the lights dropped for the storm scene.
audience.basic: The people watching gasped at the storm scene.

author.simple: The person who writes a book, play, or other text.
author.detailed: An author shapes plot, voice, and point of view. Naming the author helps you discuss choices instead of treating a book as if it wrote itself.
author.example: The author leaves the last letter unfinished so readers must infer the ending.
author.basic: The writer does not finish the last letter.

background.simple: The earlier facts or setting that help you understand an event.
background.detailed: Background information explains what happened before the main story, such as why a town already had a water shortage.
background.example: The background to the strike was a long drought that had already cut farm jobs.
background.basic: The strike happened after a long dry time.

barrier.simple: Something that blocks movement, access, or progress.
barrier.detailed: A barrier can be a fence, a language, or an unfair rule. HASS writing asks who built it and who is kept out.
barrier.zh: 障碍；壁垒；阻挡通行或进展的事物
barrier.example: The Great Dividing Range was a barrier to early travel between the coast and inland farms.
barrier.basic: The mountains made inland travel hard.

basis.simple: The main idea or evidence that something is built on.
basis.detailed: A conclusion needs a sound basis, such as repeated trials or a reliable source. If the basis is weak, the whole claim wobbles.
basis.example: The basis for our conclusion was three trials with the same thermometer.
basis.basic: We used three trials to back the conclusion.

behaviour.simple: The way a person, animal, or system usually acts.
behaviour.detailed: Scientists record behaviour they can see, such as how magpies defend a nest. In class, behaviour also means how people treat others.
behaviour.example: We recorded magpie behaviour on the oval for ten minutes after the bell.
behaviour.basic: We watched what the magpies did after the bell.

boundary.simple: A line that marks the edge of a place or a rule.
boundary.detailed: A boundary can be a river, a fence, or a limit on what is allowed. Maps and laws both use boundaries to show where one area ends.
boundary.example: The creek forms the boundary between the school oval and the reserve.
boundary.basic: The creek sits on the edge of the oval.

campaign.simple: An organised set of actions meant to win support or cause change.
campaign.detailed: A campaign can be for school captain, for recycling, or for a new law. It uses messages, events, and people working together over time.
campaign.zh: 运动；有组织的宣传或行动
campaign.example: The student campaign for tap-water stations used posters in every stairwell.
campaign.basic: Students put up posters about drinking tap water.

category.simple: A group of things that share a common feature.
category.detailed: You sort ideas, animals, or books into a category so patterns are easier to see. Name the shared feature, not just the group label.
category.example: Put each waste item into a category before you mark the tally chart.
category.basic: Sort the rubbish into groups first.

cause.simple: The reason something happens, coming before the result.
cause.detailed: A cause comes before an effect. Science writing looks for a real cause you can test, not just something that happened at the same time.
cause.zh: 原因；导致某事发生的因素
cause.example: The likely cause of the wilted seedlings was the weekend heatwave.
cause.basic: The seedlings wilted because it was so hot.

character.simple: A person or creature in a story, or the kind of person someone is.
character.detailed: A character has motives, relationships, and a way of speaking. In literary work you study how the writer builds that person on the page.
character.example: The quietest character in the play makes the bravest choice in the last scene.
character.basic: The quiet person in the play does something brave.

characteristic.simple: A typical feature that helps you recognise something.
characteristic.detailed: A characteristic of a metal might be that it conducts heat. Scientists list characteristics so living things or materials can be compared fairly.
characteristic.example: A key characteristic of the mystery rock was that it scratched glass.
characteristic.basic: The rock was hard enough to scratch glass.

choice.simple: The act of picking one option, or the option you pick.
choice.detailed: A choice has consequences. Academic writing explains why a choice was made and what else could have been selected.
choice.example: Our choice of cardboard instead of foam reduced waste from the model bridge.
choice.basic: We picked cardboard instead of foam.

circumstance.simple: A fact or condition that surrounds an event and helps explain it.
circumstance.detailed: Circumstances include time, place, weather, and people's needs. Historians judge an action by the circumstance people faced, not only by today's rules.
circumstance.zh: 情况；环境；围绕事件的具体条件
circumstance.example: The circumstance of a long drought made the water restrictions easier to understand.
circumstance.basic: The long dry spell helped explain the water rules.

citizen.simple: A person who belongs to a country or town and has rights and duties there.
citizen.detailed: A citizen can vote, follow laws, and take part in community life. HASS lessons ask how people become citizens and what fairness requires.
citizen.zh: 公民；享有权利并承担义务的成员
citizen.example: Every citizen in the town could speak at the council meeting about the new path.
citizen.basic: People from the town could speak at the meeting.

community.simple: A group of people who live in the same place or share a common interest.
community.detailed: A community can be a suburb, a sporting club, or a language group. It is held together by shared places, rules, and care for one another.
community.zh: 社区；群体；有共同生活或兴趣的一群人
community.example: The local community planted trees along the creek after the last flood.
community.basic: People from the area planted trees after the flood.

concept.simple: An idea that helps you understand a bigger topic.
concept.detailed: A concept such as fairness or energy is more than one example. You explain a concept by defining it and showing how it works in new cases.
concept.zh: 概念；帮助理解主题的核心想法
concept.example: The concept of a fair test means only one variable changes at a time.
concept.basic: A fair test changes only one thing.

condition.simple: The state something is in, or a requirement that must be met.
condition.detailed: Scientists describe the condition of a habitat, such as wet or polluted. A condition can also be a rule: you may go if a condition is satisfied.
condition.example: The dry condition of the soil explained why the seedlings needed extra water.
condition.basic: The soil was so dry that the plants needed water.

conflict.simple: A serious disagreement or struggle between people or ideas.
conflict.detailed: Conflict can be a war, a family argument, or two goals that cannot both be met. HASS writing looks at causes, power, and how conflict is resolved.
conflict.example: The conflict over river water grew after both towns needed more for irrigation.
conflict.basic: The two towns argued about river water.

connection.simple: A link that joins people, ideas, places, or events.
connection.detailed: A connection can be a trade route, a family tie, or a cause linked to an effect. Good writing makes the connection explicit.
connection.example: There is a clear connection between extra shade and cooler playground seats.
connection.basic: More shade makes the seats cooler.

content.simple: The information or ideas inside a text, not the cover or layout.
content.detailed: When you judge content, you look at what a page actually says. A colourful poster can still have thin content if the facts are missing.
content.zh: 内容；文本中的信息或思想
content.example: The marker praised the content of the report even though the diagrams were plain.
content.basic: The report had good information inside.

control.simple: The part of a test you keep the same so the comparison is fair.
control.detailed: In a fair test, a control is the unchanged comparison, or a variable you hold steady. It helps you see whether the one thing you changed really mattered.
control.zh: 对照；控制（实验中保持不变的部分）
control.example: The pot with no fertiliser was the control in our seedling trial.
control.basic: One pot had no fertiliser so we could compare.

culture.simple: The shared customs, stories, languages, and ways of life of a group.
culture.detailed: Culture includes food, ceremony, art, and daily habits. Australian HASS studies many cultures, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures.
culture.zh: 文化；一个群体共享的习俗、语言与生活方式
culture.example: Dance, language, and fishing knowledge are all part of the culture of that island community.
culture.basic: Dance and language are part of how that community lives.

cycle.simple: A sequence of events that repeats in a set order.
cycle.detailed: The water cycle and life cycles are repeating systems. A diagram of a cycle should show how the last step leads back to the first.
cycle.zh: 循环；按固定顺序重复的过程
cycle.example: Our poster showed how evaporation starts the next turn of the water cycle.
cycle.basic: The poster showed water changing and coming back again.

data.simple: Facts or measurements you collect to answer a question.
data.detailed: Data can be numbers, yes/no tallies, or careful notes. You do not change data to fit a guess; you explain what the data actually show.
data.zh: 数据；为回答问题而收集的事实或测量值
data.example: Our data showed the shaded thermometer stayed two degrees cooler at noon.
data.basic: The numbers showed the shaded spot was cooler.

decision.simple: A choice you make after thinking about the options.
decision.detailed: A decision can be personal or official. Academic writing explains the reasons for a decision and who is affected by it.
decision.example: The council's decision to close the track followed three rockfalls in one month.
decision.basic: The council closed the track after the rockfalls.

detail.simple: A small, precise piece of information that makes an idea clearer.
detail.detailed: A useful detail is specific: a time, a colour, a measurement. Too few details make writing vague; too many can hide the main point.
detail.zh: 细节；具体而精确的信息
detail.example: One telling detail was the muddy watermark halfway up the classroom wall.
detail.basic: The muddy line on the wall was a useful clue.

device.simple: A writing technique an author uses to shape meaning or feeling.
device.detailed: A literary device might be repetition, a metaphor, or a sudden short sentence. Name the device and explain the effect on the reader.
device.zh: 手法；作者用来制造效果的写作技巧
device.example: Repetition is the device that makes the last stanza feel like a drumbeat.
device.basic: Repeating words makes the last stanza sound like a drum.

difference.simple: A way in which two things are not the same.
difference.detailed: You describe a difference by naming both sides and the feature you compared. In data, a difference should be large enough to notice.
difference.example: The main difference between the two soils was how quickly water drained away.
difference.basic: The two soils did not drain at the same speed.

difficulty.simple: Something that makes a task hard to complete.
difficulty.detailed: A difficulty can be a missing tool, a confusing question, or a steep slope. Name the difficulty so you can plan a way around it.
difficulty.example: The main difficulty was keeping the rain gauge level on the sloping roof.
difficulty.basic: It was hard to keep the rain gauge level.

disadvantage.simple: A feature that makes an option weaker or less helpful.
disadvantage.detailed: In an argument, a disadvantage is a real cost or drawback. Fair writing admits a disadvantage of your own plan, then explains why it is still worth choosing.
disadvantage.example: A disadvantage of extra canteen packaging is the extra bin overflow after sport.
disadvantage.basic: Extra packaging makes the bins overflow.

discussion.simple: A careful talk or written exchange of ideas on a topic.
discussion.detailed: A discussion lets people share reasons, ask questions, and test ideas. It is more organised than a chat and fairer than a one-person speech.
discussion.zh: 讨论；就某一主题交换看法
discussion.example: Our discussion of the novel focused on whether the narrator could be trusted.
discussion.basic: We talked about whether to trust the narrator.

effect.simple: What happens afterwards as a result of a cause.
effect.detailed: An effect comes after a cause and can be measured or observed. Science writing keeps cause and effect in a clear order.
effect.zh: 结果；效应；由原因引起的变化
effect.example: The effect of the extra mulch was cooler, damper soil under the tomato plants.
effect.basic: The mulch made the soil cooler and damper.

effort.simple: The hard work and attention you put into a task.
effort.detailed: Effort is energy and attention, not just luck. Teachers and coaches notice sustained effort even before the final mark appears.
effort.zh: 努力；付出的心力或体力
effort.example: The team's effort in rehearsals showed on the night of the drama performance.
effort.basic: The team had worked hard before the play.

element.simple: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.
element.detailed: Oxygen and iron are elements because each is made of one type of atom. Water is not an element because it is made of hydrogen and oxygen joined together.
element.zh: 元素；只由一种原子构成的纯净物
element.example: Water is not a pure element because it is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
element.basic: Water is made from more than one simple substance.

energy.simple: The capacity to make things move, heat up, or change.
energy.detailed: Energy can be stored, transferred, or transformed, but it is not created from nothing. Year 5–6 science tracks where energy goes in a system.
energy.zh: 能量；使物体运动、发热或变化的能力
energy.example: The spinning turbine changed moving water into electrical energy for the model town.
energy.basic: The moving water helped make electricity.

error.simple: A mistake in a measurement, method, or calculation.
error.detailed: An error can come from a misread scale or a skipped step. Scientists look for error so they can improve the method next time.
error.example: A parallax error made the first meniscus reading look higher than it was.
error.basic: We read the water line from the wrong angle.

event.simple: Something that happens, especially something notable.
event.detailed: An event can be a flood, an election, or a sports carnival. Historians ask when the event occurred, who was involved, and why it mattered.
event.example: Federation was the event that joined six colonies into one nation in 1901.
event.basic: In 1901 the colonies joined to make one nation.

example.simple: A specific case that shows what a general idea means.
example.detailed: A strong example is concrete and relevant. One clear example often teaches more than a vague list of claims.
example.example: A yabby in the creek sample is one example of an animal that needs clean water.
example.basic: A yabby shows that the water must be fairly clean.

exchange.simple: The act of giving one thing and receiving another.
exchange.detailed: People exchange goods, letters, or ideas. In HASS, an exchange can be trade, a treaty gift, or the sharing of knowledge.
exchange.example: The museum display showed an exchange of fish hooks for woven bags between coastal groups.
exchange.basic: People swapped fish hooks for woven bags.

experience.simple: Something you have lived through, or the knowledge gained from it.
experience.detailed: A character's experience shapes how they see danger or friendship. First-hand experience is different from something you only read about.
experience.example: The narrator's experience of getting lost makes later jokes about maps feel sharper.
experience.basic: Because she got lost, the map jokes feel more serious.

experiment.simple: A planned test used to answer a scientific question.
experiment.detailed: An experiment changes one factor, keeps others steady, and records what happens. It is more than a casual try.
experiment.zh: 实验；为回答科学问题而做的有计划测试
experiment.example: The ice-cube experiment compared wrapping, shade, and foil under the same sun.
experiment.basic: We tested three ways of keeping ice from melting.

explanation.simple: A clear account of why something happens or what it means.
explanation.detailed: A good explanation uses reasons and evidence, not only a label. Science and reading tasks both ask you to write the explanation in your own words.
explanation.example: Her explanation of the rust used both the wet cotton wool and the exposed iron.
explanation.basic: She said the iron rusted because it stayed wet.

feature.simple: A noticeable part or quality of a place, object, or living thing.
feature.detailed: A feature might be a river bend, a bird's beak, or a heading on a page. Describing features helps you classify and compare.
feature.zh: 特征；显著的部分或性状
feature.example: A sharp ridge was the most obvious feature on the contour map of the reserve.
feature.basic: The map showed a sharp ridge most clearly.

figure.simple: A number, or a labelled diagram in a science text.
figure.detailed: In reports, a figure is often a graph or drawing with a caption. The word can also mean a number you have measured or calculated.
figure.zh: 数字；图表；科学文本中的图示
figure.example: The figure numbered 3 in the booklet shows how the shadow shortened toward midday.
figure.basic: The third picture shows the shadow getting shorter.

finding.simple: A result you discover after an investigation.
finding.detailed: A finding is more than a guess; it is what the evidence showed. Write findings in plain language before you add extra interpretation.
finding.example: Our main finding was that the shaded tray lost far less water by Friday.
finding.basic: We found that the shaded tray stayed wetter.

force.simple: A push or pull that can change an object's motion or shape.
force.detailed: Forces include gravity, friction, and magnetism. A force has size and direction, which you can show with arrows on a diagram.
force.zh: 力；能改变物体运动或形状的推或拉
force.example: A greater force on the trolley made it travel farther across the smooth floor.
force.basic: A harder push made the trolley go farther.

function.simple: The job something is designed or adapted to do.
function.detailed: The function of roots is to take in water; the function of a heading is to guide a reader. Form and function often fit together.
function.zh: 功能；作用；某物被用来做的事
function.example: The function of the waxy coating is to reduce water loss from the leaf.
function.basic: The waxy coating helps the leaf keep water.

goal.simple: A result you plan carefully and work toward.
goal.detailed: A goal is specific enough to check. Academic tasks often ask you to set a goal, then review whether your method reached it.
goal.zh: 目标；努力要达到的结果
goal.example: Our goal for the reading week was to finish one non-fiction book each.
goal.basic: We each wanted to finish a non-fiction book.

growth.simple: An increase in size, number, or development.
growth.detailed: Growth can be a seedling getting taller or a town gaining people. Science writing measures growth instead of only saying something 'got bigger'.
growth.example: The graph of plant growth flattened after we stopped watering in week three.
growth.basic: The plants stopped getting taller when we stopped watering.

habit.simple: An action you repeat so often it becomes usual.
habit.detailed: A habit can help, such as washing hands, or harm, such as wasting paper. Scientists also study feeding habits of animals.
habit.example: The possum's night-time habit of raiding the fruit bowl showed up on the camera.
habit.basic: The possum kept taking fruit at night.

image.simple: A picture in words or in the mind that a text creates.
image.detailed: An image can be a photograph or a phrase such as 'a sky the colour of tin'. Literary study asks what the image makes the reader feel or notice.
image.zh: 意象；画面；文字在头脑中形成的图景
image.example: The image of boots filling with creek water made the crossing feel colder.
image.basic: The line about wet boots made the crossing feel cold.

importance.simple: The quality of mattering or making a real difference.
importance.detailed: You show importance by explaining who is affected and what would change if the thing were missing. Do not just call something important.
importance.example: The report explained the importance of shade for younger students at lunch.
importance.basic: The report said shade really matters at lunch.

individual.simple: One person, considered separately from the group.
individual.detailed: Laws and stories often balance the rights of an individual with the needs of a community. The word stresses one person, not a crowd.
individual.example: Each individual in the survey gave a different reason for walking to school.
individual.basic: Each person had a different reason for walking.

industry.simple: The businesses that make or provide the same kind of goods or services.
industry.detailed: The wool industry, mining industry, or tourism industry groups related work. HASS asks how an industry changes jobs, land, and towns.
industry.example: The gold industry turned quiet valleys into crowded tent towns almost overnight.
industry.basic: Gold mining quickly filled the valleys with tents.

information.simple: Facts or details that tell you about something.
information.detailed: Information can be spoken, written, or shown in a graph. Useful information is accurate, relevant, and from a source you can check.
information.zh: 信息；关于某事物的事实或资料
information.example: We gathered information from the Bureau of Meteorology, not from a random blog.
information.basic: We used weather facts from a trusted site.

inquiry.simple: A careful investigation that seeks answers to a question.
inquiry.detailed: An inquiry uses sources, evidence, and follow-up questions. Australian classrooms run inquiries in HASS and science, not just one-off quizzes.
inquiry.zh: 探究；为回答问题而进行的调查
inquiry.example: Our Federation inquiry asked why some colonies were slower to join than others.
inquiry.basic: We asked why some colonies joined later.

instruction.simple: A direction that tells you how to do a task.
instruction.detailed: An instruction should be clear enough to follow without guessing. In tests, missing one instruction can change the whole answer.
instruction.example: The first instruction on the paper was to read the whole question before writing.
instruction.basic: The paper said to read the whole question first.

issue.simple: An important problem or topic people disagree about.
issue.detailed: An issue such as water use or housing has more than one side. HASS writing names the issue, the groups involved, and possible responses.
issue.zh: 议题；有争议的重要问题
issue.example: Rubbish in the harbour became a public issue after the storm washed bins into the water.
issue.basic: People started worrying about harbour rubbish after the storm.

judgement.simple: A careful opinion formed after weighing evidence.
judgement.detailed: A judgement is more than a quick like or dislike. In argument writing you make a judgement and show the reasons that support it.
judgement.zh: 判断；在权衡证据后形成的看法
judgement.example: After both sides spoke, the class made a judgement about which plan was fairer to younger students.
judgement.basic: The class decided which plan was fairer.

knowledge.simple: Understanding you have learned and can use.
knowledge.detailed: Knowledge is more than memorised words; you can apply it in a new problem. First Nations knowledge of Country is a living body of learning.
knowledge.zh: 知识；已经掌握并能运用的理解
knowledge.example: Local knowledge of the tides saved the group from crossing at the wrong time.
knowledge.basic: People who knew the tides kept the group safe.

language.simple: The words and patterns people use to share meaning.
language.detailed: Language includes vocabulary, grammar, and tone. Literary study looks at how language choices create mood, character, and theme.
language.zh: 语言；人们用来交流意义的词语和方式
language.example: The playful language in the first stanza turns sharp when the storm arrives.
language.basic: The words start fun and then feel serious in the storm.

layer.simple: One thickness of material lying over or under another.
layer.detailed: Soil, rock, and the atmosphere form layers. A diagram should show the order of each layer and what it is made of.
layer.zh: 层；一层叠在另一层上的物质
layer.example: The top layer of soil was darker because it held more decayed leaves.
layer.basic: The soil on top looked darker from old leaves.

leader.simple: A person who guides a group and helps it make decisions.
leader.detailed: A leader can be elected, appointed, or followed because of respect. HASS asks how a leader gained power and whom they served.
leader.zh: 领导者；带领群体做决定的人
leader.example: The team chose a leader who listened before giving instructions on the hike.
leader.basic: The team picked someone who listened first.

material.simple: What an object is made of, such as wood, metal, or plastic.
material.detailed: A material has properties you can test, such as hardness or absorbency. Science writing names the material instead of saying 'stuff'.
material.zh: 材料；物质；物体由什么制成
material.example: Cotton was the only material in the test that soaked up the whole puddle.
material.basic: Only the cotton soaked up all the water.

meaning.simple: What a word, action, or text is meant to express.
meaning.detailed: Meaning can be literal or suggested. In literature you explain meaning by pointing to words in the text, not only to your own feelings.
meaning.zh: 意义；含义；想要表达的意思
meaning.example: The meaning of the last line changes if you read the letter as a warning.
meaning.basic: The last line feels different if the letter is a warning.

message.simple: The main idea a text is trying to communicate.
message.detailed: A message can be stated or implied. Ask what the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do after reading.
message.zh: 信息；主旨；文本想传达的意思
message.example: The message of the picture book is that small acts of care still count.
message.basic: The book wants us to see that small kind acts matter.

model.simple: A simplified version used to explain how something works.
model.detailed: A model can be a drawing, a 3D build, or a set of rules. It is useful even if it leaves out some real-world detail.
model.zh: 模型；用来解释事物如何运作的简化版本
model.example: Our cardboard model of the harbour showed why the tide gates had to open both ways.
model.basic: The cardboard harbour helped us see how the gates work.

movement.simple: A group of people acting together to cause social or political change.
movement.detailed: A movement shares a goal, such as voting rights or environmental protection. HASS writing asks who joined, what they demanded, and what changed.
movement.zh: 运动；为推动社会或政治变革而联合行动的群体
movement.example: The conservation movement grew after people saw photos of oil on the beach.
movement.basic: More people wanted to protect nature after the oil photos.

narrative.simple: A story that tells what happened, real or imagined.
narrative.detailed: A narrative has events in an order, a voice, and usually characters. It can be a novel, a spoken account, or a historical story.
narrative.zh: 叙事；讲述事情经过的故事
narrative.example: The camp narrative slows down at the river so readers feel every slippery step.
narrative.basic: The camp story spends a long time on the river crossing.

network.simple: A connected group of people, places, or lines that work together.
network.detailed: A rail network joins towns; a support network joins people. HASS maps often show how a network carries goods, news, or help.
network.zh: 网络；相互连接并协同运作的系统
network.example: The rail network let inland wheat reach the port before it spoiled.
network.basic: The trains helped wheat get to the port in time.

object.simple: A physical thing you can see or touch in science.
object.detailed: In science an object has properties such as mass and material. Keep this noun sense separate from the verb that means 'to disagree'.
object.zh: 物体；可以看见或触摸的东西
object.example: Each group tested one metal object to see whether it was attracted to the magnet.
object.basic: Each group tested one metal thing with the magnet.

opinion.simple: A personal view that is not proven as fact.
opinion.detailed: An opinion can still be well supported. In argument writing you separate opinion from evidence so readers can judge your case.
opinion.zh: 意见；看法；尚未被证明为事实的观点
opinion.example: It is my opinion that the oval should stay open, but I still need evidence about safety.
opinion.basic: I think the oval should stay open, and I need facts too.

opportunity.simple: A good chance to do something useful or gain something.
opportunity.detailed: An opportunity can be a new job, a speaking turn, or a gap in the weather. HASS asks who gets an opportunity and who is left out.
opportunity.zh: 机会；做某事或获得某物的有利时机
opportunity.example: The excursion was an opportunity to see original Federation documents, not only copies.
opportunity.basic: The trip let us see the real Federation papers.

option.simple: One possible choice among two or more others.
option.detailed: An option is available; you may take it or leave it. Academic writing compares options using the same criteria.
option.zh: 选项；可供选择的一种方案
option.example: A later bus was the safest option after the storm warning.
option.basic: Taking a later bus was the safest choice.

outcome.simple: The result at the end of a process or decision.
outcome.detailed: An outcome can be planned or surprising. After a project you compare the outcome with the original aim.
outcome.zh: 结果；一项过程或决定最终产生的局面
outcome.example: The unexpected outcome was that the quieter group collected more accurate tallies.
outcome.basic: In the end the quieter group had better counts.

passage.simple: A short section of a text used for reading or analysis.
passage.detailed: A passage may be a paragraph or a page. Scholarship papers often ask you to use evidence from the passage only.
passage.zh: 选段；文章中供阅读或分析的一段
passage.example: In the second passage the narrator finally admits she hid the compass.
passage.basic: In the next part she admits she hid the compass.

pattern.simple: A repeated arrangement you can notice and describe.
pattern.detailed: A pattern can be in numbers, colours, behaviour, or weather. Once you see a pattern, you can often make a better prediction.
pattern.zh: 模式；可以识别和描述的重复安排
pattern.example: A clear pattern in the data was hotter afternoons after cloudless mornings.
pattern.basic: Hot afternoons often followed clear mornings.

period.simple: A stretch of time in history or in a process.
period.detailed: A period might be the gold rush years or the time a seed takes to germinate. Name the beginning and end if you can.
period.example: During the gold-rush period, some towns doubled in size within a year.
period.basic: In the gold-rush years some towns grew very fast.

policy.simple: An official plan for how things should be done.
policy.detailed: A school, council, or government sets a policy so decisions stay consistent. Good HASS writing asks who made the policy and who it helps.
policy.zh: 政策；官方制定的行事计划
policy.example: The new hat policy applies on the oval as well as in the undercroft.
policy.basic: The new hat rule is for the oval and the undercroft.

population.simple: All the people or living things in a particular place.
population.detailed: A population can be counted, mapped, and compared over time. Scientists also talk about a population of frogs in one creek.
population.zh: 人口；某一地区的全部人或生物
population.example: The frog population in the wetland rose after the reeds were replanted.
population.basic: More frogs lived in the wetland after the reeds grew back.

position.simple: The view you take on an issue in a debate.
position.detailed: Your position is the side you argue for. State it early, then support it so readers are not guessing what you want.
position.zh: 立场；在争论中所持的观点
position.example: My position is that phones should stay in bags unless a teacher asks for research.
position.basic: I think phones should stay in bags most of the time.

possibility.simple: Something that might happen or might be true.
possibility.detailed: A possibility is not certain. Science writing treats a possibility as an idea to test, not as a finished fact.
possibility.zh: 可能性；可能发生或可能属实的事
possibility.example: There is a possibility that the missing lunch orders were left on the earlier bus.
possibility.basic: The lunch orders might have been left on the early bus.

practice.simple: A usual way of doing something, or repeated work that builds skill.
practice.detailed: Classroom practice can mean a habit, such as drafting before publishing. It can also mean rehearsal that makes a skill more reliable.
practice.example: Daily practice of times tables made Friday's mental quiz feel much calmer.
practice.basic: Doing tables every day made Friday's quiz easier.

pressure.simple: A force pushing on a surface, or a strong demand that pushes people.
pressure.detailed: In science, pressure is force spread over an area, such as air pressure. People also feel pressure when time or expectations push them.
pressure.zh: 压力；作用于表面的力，或对人的紧迫要求
pressure.example: Higher air pressure in the balloon made the walls feel tighter under our hands.
pressure.basic: The balloon felt tighter when we pumped in more air.

principle.simple: A basic rule or belief that guides action.
principle.detailed: A principle is more general than one classroom rule. Fairness as a principle can guide many different decisions.
principle.zh: 原则；指导行动的基本准则
principle.example: The principle of a fair test is that only one variable changes at a time.
principle.basic: In a fair test you change only one thing.

procedure.simple: A planned sequence of steps for doing a task.
procedure.detailed: A procedure tells you what to do first, next, and last. Science methods are procedures so another group can repeat the test.
procedure.zh: 程序；完成任务的步骤顺序
procedure.example: The fire-drill procedure is to leave bags, walk to the oval, and wait for the roll.
procedure.basic: In a fire drill we leave bags and walk to the oval.

product.simple: Something made by a process, person, or living thing.
product.detailed: A product can be a loaf of bread, a chemical formed in a reaction, or a finished poster. Name what was made and how.
product.zh: 产物；产品；过程制造出来的东西
product.example: Rust was the brown product that formed on the wet iron nails.
product.basic: The wet nails turned brown on the outside.

progress.simple: Forward movement toward a goal or a better state.
progress.detailed: Progress can be a better draft, a faster time, or a town gaining a library. Measure progress against a starting point.
progress.example: The class made real progress once each group had a clear job on the poster.
progress.basic: The poster improved after everyone had a job.

project.simple: A planned piece of work with a clear aim and end point.
project.detailed: A project has tasks, materials, and a deadline. In school it is usually longer than one lesson and ends with a product or presentation.
project.zh: 课题；有明确目标和终点的计划性工作
project.example: Our science project compared three ways of keeping a lunchbox cool.
project.basic: We tested three ways to keep lunch cool.

property.simple: A quality of a material that you can observe or test.
property.detailed: Hardness, flexibility, and conductivity are properties. Do not confuse this science sense with land or buildings that someone owns.
property.zh: 特性；属性；材料可观察或测试的性质
property.example: Flexibility was the property that made the rubber band more useful than the stick.
property.basic: The rubber band was more useful because it could bend.

purpose.simple: The reason something is done, written, or made.
purpose.detailed: A text's purpose might be to inform, persuade, or entertain. Naming the purpose helps you judge whether the writing works.
purpose.zh: 目的；某事被做或被制造的原因
purpose.example: The purpose of the opening statistic was to shock readers into caring about food waste.
purpose.basic: The first number was there to make readers care about waste.

quality.simple: How good something is, or a feature that something has.
quality.detailed: Quality can mean standard of work, such as a high-quality explanation. It can also mean a trait, such as the quality of honesty.
quality.zh: 质量；品质；事物所具有的特性
quality.example: The quality of the creek water improved after the cattle were fenced out.
quality.basic: The creek water got cleaner after the cattle were kept back.

range.simple: The spread of things from the lowest to the highest, or a variety.
range.detailed: A range can be a set of temperatures, ages, or choices. Academic writing uses range to show how wide a set of results really is.
range.zh: 范围；幅度；从最低到最高的跨度
range.example: The temperature range on the oval was eight degrees between shade and sun.
range.basic: Shade and sun on the oval differed by eight degrees.

reason.simple: A fact or idea that explains why something is true or why you think it.
reason.detailed: A reason supports a claim. In argument writing, each reason should be clear enough that a reader can agree or disagree with it.
reason.zh: 理由；原因；解释为何如此的依据
reason.example: The best reason for later start times was the survey of tired Year 6 students.
reason.basic: The tiredness survey was the strongest point for a later start.

relationship.simple: The way two people, groups, or things are connected.
relationship.detailed: A relationship can be friendly, official, or cause-and-effect. HASS and science both ask you to describe the relationship, not only name the pair.
relationship.zh: 关系；两者之间的关联方式
relationship.example: The graph shows the relationship between extra study time and fewer errors.
relationship.basic: The graph shows that more study went with fewer mistakes.

resource.simple: Something useful that people can use to meet a need.
resource.detailed: Water, timber, money, and skilled workers are resources. HASS asks whether a resource is renewable and who controls it.
resource.zh: 资源；可用来满足需要的有用之物
resource.example: Fresh water is the resource the inland town must protect first in a drought.
resource.basic: The inland town has to look after its fresh water in a drought.

result.simple: What you get at the end of a test, action, or process.
result.detailed: A result should be reported honestly, even if it surprises you. Then you can explain the result using the method and the conditions.
result.zh: 结果；测试或行动最终得到的情况
result.example: The surprising result was that the cheaper insulation kept the ice solid longer.
result.basic: We were surprised that the cheaper wrapping worked better.

risk.simple: The chance that something harmful could happen.
risk.detailed: A risk has both likelihood and seriousness. Science and safety plans try to lower risk without pretending danger has vanished.
risk.zh: 风险；有害事情发生的可能性
risk.example: There is a higher risk of slipping when the rocks are covered in green algae.
risk.basic: You are more likely to slip on the slimy rocks.

role.simple: The job or part a person or thing has in a group or system.
role.detailed: A role can be school captain, narrator, or the role of roots in a plant. Naming a role helps you explain responsibility and purpose.
role.zh: 角色；职责；在群体或系统中的作用
role.example: The role of the chairperson is to keep the debate fair, not to win it.
role.basic: The chairperson should keep the debate fair.

sample.simple: A small part taken to represent a larger whole.
sample.detailed: You test a sample of water or soil because you cannot test the whole creek. A fair sample should not be chosen only to prove a guess.
sample.zh: 样本；用来代表整体的一小部分
sample.example: Each group collected a water sample from a different bend in the creek.
sample.basic: Each group took some water from a different bend.

scale.simple: How large or small something is compared with a standard, or a set of marks for measuring.
scale.detailed: Map scale shows real distance. A measuring scale on a cylinder shows volume. Both help you compare sizes fairly.
scale.zh: 尺度；比例；用于测量的刻度
scale.example: Using the map scale, we calculated that the reserve walk is about three kilometres.
scale.basic: The map helped us work out that the walk is about three kilometres.

section.simple: A distinct part of a text, place, or object.
section.detailed: A section has its own job, such as a methods section or a section of the oval. Headings help readers find each section quickly.
section.zh: 部分；章节；相对独立的一块
section.example: The methods section must list every material, including the spare thermometers.
section.basic: The methods part should list every material.

sequence.simple: The order in which things happen or should be done.
sequence.detailed: A sequence can be a life-cycle order or the steps in a method. If you change the sequence, the result may change too.
sequence.zh: 顺序；序列；事情发生或应完成的次序
sequence.example: Write the life-cycle sequence from egg to adult before you colour the arrows.
sequence.basic: Put the life-cycle stages in order first.

setting.simple: The time and place in which a story happens.
setting.detailed: Setting includes weather, buildings, and atmosphere. Changing the setting can change a character's choices and the whole mood.
setting.zh: 背景；故事发生的时间和地点
setting.example: A flooded caravan park is a tense setting for a story about a lost dog.
setting.basic: A flooded caravan park makes the lost-dog story feel tense.

solution.simple: A mixture made when one substance dissolves evenly in another.
solution.detailed: Salt water is a solution if the salt can no longer be seen as grains. In science, keep this meaning separate from 'an answer to a problem'.
solution.zh: 溶液；一种物质均匀溶解于另一种物质形成的混合物
solution.example: The salt solution looked clear even though we had added a whole spoonful.
solution.basic: The salty water looked clear after the grains disappeared.

source.simple: The place, person, or text that information or a material comes from.
source.detailed: A source can be a river's beginning, a witness, or a website. Academic work names the source so others can check it.
source.zh: 来源；信息或材料的出处
source.example: A diary from 1901 is a stronger source for Federation feelings than a modern cartoon.
source.basic: An old diary tells us more about 1901 feelings than a new cartoon.

stage.simple: One step or phase inside a longer process.
stage.detailed: A stage has its own features, such as the pupa stage of a butterfly. Naming the stage helps you explain what happens next.
stage.zh: 阶段；较长过程中的一个步骤
stage.example: At this stage of the inquiry we only collect sources; we do not write conclusions yet.
stage.basic: Right now we are only collecting sources.

standard.simple: An agreed level of quality used for judging work or safety.
standard.detailed: A standard tells you what 'good enough' looks like. Tests, sports, and science methods all use standards so judgements stay fair.
standard.zh: 标准；用来评判质量或安全的约定水平
standard.example: The safety standard for the Bunsen burner is tied hair and clear benches.
standard.basic: For the burner you need tied hair and a clear bench.

statement.simple: A clear sentence that says something is true or that you believe it.
statement.detailed: A statement can be a fact, a claim, or an official announcement. In argument, you test a statement instead of accepting it because it sounds confident.
statement.zh: 陈述；声明；表明观点或事实的句子
statement.example: The first statement in her speech was that every student deserves shade at lunch.
statement.basic: She began by saying every student should have shade at lunch.

subject.simple: A topic of study or the thing a text is about.
subject.detailed: A subject can be science, or the subject of a paragraph. Keep the focus on the subject so extra stories do not wander away.
subject.zh: 学科；主题；文本所讨论的对象
subject.example: The subject of the next chapter is how wind shapes coastal dunes.
subject.basic: The next chapter is about wind and sand dunes.

success.simple: The achievement of what you aimed to do.
success.detailed: Success can be a finished goal, a fair win, or a method that works. Define success before you start so you know what to measure.
success.example: The success of the compost bin was the rich soil we used in the winter garden.
success.basic: The compost worked because we got good soil for winter.

system.simple: A set of parts that work together as a whole.
system.detailed: A system can be the digestive system, a weather system, or a school's recycling system. Changing one part can affect the rest.
system.zh: 系统；相互配合运作的一组部分
system.example: If one pump fails, the whole irrigation system on the farm slows down.
system.basic: If one pump breaks, the farm watering slows down.

task.simple: A piece of work you are asked to complete.
task.detailed: A task has a purpose and often a time limit. Breaking a big assignment into smaller tasks makes progress easier to see.
task.zh: 任务；需要完成的一项工作
task.example: Your first task is to highlight every verb in the passage before you rewrite it.
task.basic: First, highlight the verbs, then rewrite the passage.

technique.simple: A particular skilled way of doing something.
technique.detailed: A technique is more precise than a vague 'way'. Science, sport, and art all have techniques you can practise and name.
technique.zh: 技巧；方法；做某事的专门做法
technique.example: A better pouring technique stopped the oil from coating the whole measuring cylinder.
technique.basic: Pouring more carefully kept oil off the sides of the cylinder.

term.simple: A word that has a special meaning in a subject.
term.detailed: A scientific term such as 'condensation' is more precise than everyday language. Always define a term the first time you use it in a report.
term.zh: 术语；在某一学科中有特定含义的词语
term.example: In this unit, the term 'habitat' means the place that supplies food, water, and shelter.
term.basic: Here, 'habitat' means the place an animal lives and finds what it needs.

theme.simple: The big idea a story keeps returning to.
theme.detailed: A theme is not just the topic. Friendship, courage, or belonging can be a theme if events and images keep pointing to that idea.
theme.zh: 主题；故事反复指向的核心思想
theme.example: Belonging is the theme that links the lonely first chapter to the final team scene.
theme.basic: The story keeps coming back to the idea of belonging.

theory.simple: An explanation that scientists use because lots of evidence supports it.
theory.detailed: A theory is stronger than a guess. It explains many results and can still be tested. It is not 'just a theory' in the everyday sense.
theory.zh: 理论；有大量证据支持的科学解释
theory.example: Germ theory is the theory that tiny living things can cause many diseases.
theory.basic: Scientists explain many illnesses by talking about tiny living things.

topic.simple: The subject you are reading, writing, or talking about.
topic.detailed: A topic should be focused enough to cover well. 'Water in our town' is a clearer topic than 'the environment' on its own.
topic.zh: 话题；正在阅读、写作或讨论的主题
topic.example: Our essay topic is how shade sails changed play on the senior oval.
topic.basic: We are writing about shade sails on the senior oval.

trend.simple: A general direction of change over time.
trend.detailed: A trend can be rising temperatures or falling library loans. You need several points, not one unusual day, before you name a trend.
trend.zh: 趋势；一段时间内变化的总体方向
trend.example: The graph shows a trend toward drier springs in the last twenty years.
trend.basic: Springs have been getting drier over the last twenty years.

view.simple: An opinion you hold about an issue or idea.
view.detailed: A view is a way of seeing a problem. Fair argument writing presents more than one view before judging which is stronger.
view.zh: 观点；对某一问题的看法
view.example: An opposing view is that extra sport time would cut into reading support.
view.basic: Some people say extra sport would take time from reading.

volume.simple: The amount of space a liquid or object takes up.
volume.detailed: Volume is measured in millilitres or cubic centimetres, not in mass. Use the scale on a measuring cylinder and read the meniscus at eye level.
volume.zh: 体积；液体或物体所占的空间
volume.example: We recorded the volume of water left in each cylinder after the sponge test.
volume.basic: We wrote down how much water was left after the sponge test.

access.simple: The chance or right to reach or use something.
access.detailed: Access can mean a path into a reserve or the right to use a library computer. Academic writing asks who has access and who is blocked.
access.zh: 准入；使用或到达某物的机会或权利
access.example: Weekend access to the library computers helped students without home internet.
access.basic: Opening the library on Saturday helped students without internet at home.

account.simple: A report that tells what happened in an event.
account.detailed: A historical account can be a diary, a news report, or a spoken story. Compare more than one account because people remember events differently.
account.zh: 记述；对事情经过的报告
account.example: A miner’s account of the goldfields described dust, noise, and sudden fortunes.
account.basic: A miner wrote about dust, noise, and sudden riches.

acid.simple: A sour substance that can react with metals and turn indicator paper red.
acid.detailed: Lemon juice and vinegar contain acid. In science you handle acids carefully because some can burn skin or eat into metal.
acid.zh: 酸；有酸味、能使指示剂变红的物质
acid.example: Vinegar is a weak acid, so it fizzed gently on the marble chip.
acid.basic: Vinegar bubbled a little on the marble chip.

agriculture.simple: The work of growing crops and raising animals for food and other products.
agriculture.detailed: Agriculture includes farms, orchards, and grazing. HASS looks at how agriculture changes land, water use, and town jobs.
agriculture.zh: 农业；种植作物和饲养动物的生产活动
agriculture.example: Irrigation changed agriculture along the Murray by letting crops grow in drier seasons.
agriculture.basic: River water let farmers grow crops even in dry seasons.

ancestor.simple: A family member who lived in an earlier generation.
ancestor.detailed: An ancestor might be a great-grandparent or a much earlier relative. First Nations peoples also speak of ancestors in cultural and spiritual ways.
ancestor.example: The museum display showed tools an ancestor might have used on the river flats.
ancestor.basic: The museum showed old tools used by earlier family members.

artefact.simple: An object made by people in the past that we can study today.
artefact.detailed: An artefact might be a tool, pot, or piece of jewellery. Museums use artefacts as sources, and they must be handled with respect.
artefact.zh: 人工制品；过去的人制造、可供研究的物件
artefact.example: The clay fishing weight was the artefact that showed people had worked that river for generations.
artefact.basic: The old clay weight showed people had fished that river for a long time.

atmosphere.simple: The layer of gases that surrounds Earth.
atmosphere.detailed: The atmosphere holds the air we breathe and helps control temperature. Science writing may also name layers such as the troposphere.
atmosphere.zh: 大气；围绕地球的气体层
atmosphere.example: Without the atmosphere, Earth's surface would face much more harmful radiation from the sun.
atmosphere.basic: The air around Earth helps protect the surface from harsh sunlight.

authority.simple: The official power to make rules or decisions, or a trusted expert.
authority.detailed: A council has authority to set local rules. A scientist can be an authority on a topic if their knowledge is respected and checkable.
authority.zh: 权威；官方权力；可信的专家
authority.example: The local authority closed the track because falling rocks made it unsafe.
authority.basic: The council closed the track because of falling rocks.

bacteria.simple: Tiny living things, too small to see, that can help or harm other life.
bacteria.detailed: Bacteria can decompose food scraps or cause infection. They are single-celled and are not the same as viruses.
bacteria.zh: 细菌；肉眼看不见的微小生物，可有益也可有害
bacteria.example: Helpful bacteria in the compost break food scraps into dark soil.
bacteria.basic: Tiny living things in the compost help turn scraps into soil.

bias.simple: An unfair leaning toward one side that twists judgement.
bias.detailed: Bias can appear in word choice, missing facts, or a sample that was not fairly chosen. Good readers look for bias before they trust a claim.
bias.zh: 偏见；偏向一方而扭曲判断
bias.example: The flyer showed bias by quoting only shop owners who wanted more parking.
bias.basic: The flyer only used quotes from people who wanted more parking.

carbon.simple: A chemical element found in living things, fuels, and diamonds.
carbon.detailed: Carbon atoms join in many ways, so carbon appears in wood, plastic, and carbon dioxide. Year 5–6 science often tracks carbon in the air and in fuels.
carbon.zh: 碳；存在于生物、燃料和钻石中的化学元素
carbon.example: Burning the candle released carbon into the air as carbon dioxide.
carbon.basic: The burning candle sent a carbon gas into the air.

cell.simple: The tiny living unit that makes up plants, animals, and other organisms.
cell.detailed: Most living things are made of one cell or many cells. A cell can take in nutrients, grow, and, in many cases, divide.
cell.zh: 细胞；构成生物体的微小生命单位
cell.example: Under the microscope, each onion cell looked like a tiny box with a wall.
cell.basic: The onion piece looked like little boxes under the microscope.

chemical.simple: A pure substance, or a mixture, with a definite make-up you can test.
chemical.detailed: Water, salt, and vinegar are chemicals you meet every day. In the lab you use the word for substances whose properties you record carefully.
chemical.example: A colour change was the first sign that a new chemical had formed in the beaker.
chemical.basic: The liquid changed colour, so something new had formed.

climate.simple: The usual weather of a place over a long time.
climate.detailed: Climate is not one hot day; it is the pattern of temperature and rainfall over many years. Australia has many different climates.
climate.zh: 气候；一个地方长期的典型天气状况
climate.example: A desert climate can still have cold nights even when the days are burning hot.
climate.basic: Deserts can be hot by day and cold at night.

climax.simple: The most intense or important moment in a story.
climax.detailed: The climax is usually where the main conflict comes to a head. After it, the story winds toward a resolution.
climax.zh: 高潮；故事中最紧张或最关键的时刻
climax.example: The climax comes when the two sisters finally open the locked tin on the beach.
climax.basic: The most intense moment is when they open the locked tin.

colony.simple: A settlement ruled by another country, or a group of the same living things living together.
colony.detailed: In Australian HASS, a colony was a territory governed from Britain. In science, a colony can also mean a group of ants, bees, or bacteria.
colony.zh: 殖民地；群体（也可指聚居的生物）
colony.example: New South Wales began as a British colony in 1788 on land already occupied.
colony.basic: Britain started a settlement in New South Wales in 1788.

condensation.simple: The change of a gas into a liquid when it cools.
condensation.detailed: Water vapour turns into droplets on a cold window by condensation. It is the opposite process to evaporation in the water cycle.
condensation.zh: 凝结；气体遇冷变成液体
condensation.example: We saw condensation on the cold bottle as soon as it left the esky.
condensation.basic: Tiny drops formed on the cold bottle from the esky.

conductor.simple: A material that lets heat or electricity pass through it easily.
conductor.detailed: Metals are often good conductors. A wooden spoon is a poorer conductor of heat, which is why it stays cooler in a hot pot.
conductor.zh: 导体；容易传热或导电的材料
conductor.example: Copper wire is a good conductor, so the tiny bulb lit as soon as the circuit closed.
conductor.basic: The copper wire let electricity through and the bulb lit up.

conservation.simple: The careful protection of nature, resources, or special places.
conservation.detailed: Conservation can mean saving water, protecting a habitat, or looking after an old building. It is about wise use, not only locking things away.
conservation.zh: 保护；对自然、资源或特殊场所的审慎守护
conservation.example: Water conservation at school started with fixing the dripping taps near the oval.
conservation.basic: Saving water started with fixing the dripping taps.

constitution.simple: The main set of rules that says how a country is governed.
constitution.detailed: Australia's constitution explains the role of parliament, the courts, and the states. Changing it requires a special national vote called a referendum.
constitution.zh: 宪法；规定国家如何治理的根本规则
constitution.example: The Australian constitution sets out how the federal parliament is formed.
constitution.basic: Australia's main rule book says how federal parliament is formed.

council.simple: A local group elected to make decisions for a town or area.
council.detailed: A council looks after roads, parks, bins, and many local rules. It is closer to daily life than the national parliament.
council.zh: 议会；市政委员会；地方民选决策机构
council.example: The local council voted to put extra bins on the foreshore after summer.
council.basic: Town leaders voted for extra bins on the foreshore.

custom.simple: A traditional way of doing something that a group keeps over time.
custom.detailed: A custom can be a greeting, a ceremony, or a holiday meal. Customs matter because they carry meaning, not only because they are old.
custom.zh: 习俗；一个群体长期保持的传统做法
custom.example: A welcome to Country is a custom that recognises First Nations peoples as the first caretakers of the land.
custom.basic: A welcome to Country is a traditional way to recognise First Nations peoples.

democracy.simple: A system of government in which people have a say, often by voting.
democracy.detailed: In a democracy, citizens can elect leaders and speak about public issues. It also depends on fair laws and respect for rights, not only on one vote day.
democracy.zh: 民主；人民通过投票等方式参与治理的制度
democracy.example: Class elections are a small way to practise the habits of a democracy.
democracy.basic: Class elections are a small way to practise voting and fair rules.

density.simple: How much mass is packed into a certain volume.
density.detailed: A stone can have greater density than a piece of wood of the same size, so the stone sinks. Density equals mass divided by volume.
density.zh: 密度；一定体积内所含质量的多少
density.example: The metal cube had a greater density than the wooden cube of the same size.
density.basic: The metal cube was heavier than the same-sized wooden cube.

dialogue.simple: The spoken words between characters in a text or play.
dialogue.detailed: Dialogue reveals personality, conflict, and relationships. Punctuation and new lines help readers hear who is speaking.
dialogue.zh: 对话；文本或戏剧中人物之间的对白
dialogue.example: The short, snapped dialogue in the kitchen scene shows the sisters are still angry.
dialogue.basic: Their short spoken lines in the kitchen show they are still angry.

economy.simple: The system of making, buying, and selling goods and services in a place.
economy.detailed: A town's economy includes jobs, shops, farms, and trade. When one industry shrinks, the whole economy of that town can feel it.
economy.zh: 经济；一个地方生产、购买和销售的体系
economy.example: When the mill closed, the local economy lost many after-school jobs as well.
economy.basic: After the mill closed, the town had fewer jobs for families.

ecosystem.simple: A community of living things and the non-living parts they depend on.
ecosystem.detailed: An ecosystem includes plants, animals, soil, water, and climate working together. Changing one part, such as removing shade trees, can affect the rest.
ecosystem.zh: 生态系统；生物及其依存的非生物环境组成的整体
ecosystem.example: Removing the reeds damaged the creek ecosystem that the frogs depended on.
ecosystem.basic: Pulling out the reeds hurt the frogs that lived in the creek.

election.simple: A formal vote to choose a person or a decision.
election.detailed: An election can choose a student leader, a council, or a national government. Fair elections need clear rules and a secret or private vote.
election.zh: 选举；通过正式投票作出选择
election.example: The school election used paper ballots so no one could see a classmate's choice.
election.basic: Students voted on paper so choices stayed private.

empire.simple: A group of countries or lands ruled by one powerful government.
empire.detailed: An empire expands by force, settlement, or trade. HASS writing asks how an empire treated the people already living in those lands.
empire.zh: 帝国；由一个强大政府统治的多片土地
empire.example: Maps of the British empire once coloured huge parts of the world the same pink.
empire.basic: Old maps showed Britain ruling many lands across the world.

evaporation.simple: The change of a liquid into a gas, often when it is heated or left in dry air.
evaporation.detailed: Puddles shrink by evaporation. In the water cycle, evaporation lifts water into the air before condensation can form clouds.
evaporation.example: The shallow tray lost water faster because evaporation is quicker over a larger surface.
evaporation.basic: The shallow tray dried faster because more water touched the air.

exploration.simple: The act of travelling into a place to find out what is there.
exploration.detailed: Exploration can map a coast or search a creek. In Australian history, exploration stories must also include the First Nations peoples who already knew the land.
exploration.zh: 探索；考察；前往某地探明情况
exploration.example: European exploration of the inland often followed rivers already known to Aboriginal guides.
exploration.basic: Inland journeys often followed rivers that Aboriginal guides already knew.

federation.simple: The joining of separate colonies or states into one nation.
federation.detailed: Australian Federation in 1901 united six colonies under one federal parliament while states kept many powers. It is a key HASS topic in Year 6.
federation.zh: 联邦；若干殖民地或州联合成一个国家
federation.example: After federation in 1901, the new nation still had six state governments as well as a federal one.
federation.basic: After 1901 Australia had a national government and state governments.

fiction.simple: Writing that tells imagined events rather than a strictly true record.
fiction.detailed: Novels, short stories, and many plays are fiction. They can still tell truths about feelings and ideas, even when the plot is made up.
fiction.example: Even though the flood story is fiction, the fear of rising water feels true.
fiction.basic: The flood story is made up, but the fear feels real.

fossil.simple: The preserved remains or mark of a living thing from long ago.
fossil.detailed: A fossil can be bone, shell, or a footprint in rock. Fossils help scientists infer how living things and environments have changed.
fossil.zh: 化石；远古生物保存下来的遗骸或痕迹
fossil.example: The leaf fossil in the sandstone showed that a wetter forest once grew here.
fossil.basic: The leaf mark in the rock showed a wetter forest used to grow here.

friction.simple: A force that resists motion when two surfaces rub together.
friction.detailed: Friction can slow a bike or help shoes grip the oval. Smoother surfaces usually produce less friction than rough ones.
friction.zh: 摩擦；两表面相互摩擦时阻碍运动的力
friction.example: Sandpaper increased friction so the wooden block stopped sliding so easily.
friction.basic: The rough paper made the block harder to slide.

genre.simple: A type of text that follows certain familiar features.
genre.detailed: Mystery, fantasy, and information report are genres. Knowing the genre helps you predict structure, language, and what the reader expects.
genre.zh: 体裁；类型；具有某些惯用特征的文本类别
genre.example: A locked diary and hidden clues tell you the text is working in the mystery genre.
genre.basic: A locked diary and hidden clues show it is a mystery story.

government.simple: The group of people and organisations that make and carry out public rules.
government.detailed: Government can be local, state, or federal in Australia. It collects taxes, provides services, and is meant to act within the law.
government.zh: 政府；制定并执行公共规则的机构与人员
government.example: The state government funds many public hospitals, while councils look after local parks.
government.basic: The state pays for many hospitals, and councils look after parks.

habitat.simple: The natural place where a plant or animal lives and finds what it needs.
habitat.detailed: A habitat supplies food, water, shelter, and space. If a habitat is damaged, the living things that depend on it are at risk.
habitat.zh: 栖息地；动植物生活并获取所需的自然环境
habitat.example: Plastic in the wetland habitat can trap birds that come in to feed.
habitat.basic: Plastic in the wetland can trap feeding birds.

heritage.simple: Valued traditions, places, and objects passed down from earlier generations.
heritage.detailed: Heritage can be a language, a building, or a national park. Australian heritage includes First Nations heritage and later migrant heritage.
heritage.zh: 遗产；从先辈传承下来的传统、场所和物品
heritage.example: The old courthouse is part of the town's heritage and is now protected.
heritage.basic: The old courthouse is an important building from the town's past.

imagery.simple: Word pictures that appeal to the senses in a text.
imagery.detailed: Imagery uses sight, sound, smell, taste, or touch so a reader can imagine the scene. It is a cluster of images working together, not only one photo.
imagery.zh: 意象；形象描写；诉诸感官的文字画面
imagery.example: The poem's imagery of wet wool and diesel makes the cattle truck impossible to ignore.
imagery.basic: The poem's wet-wool and diesel details make the cattle truck feel real.
